claims.assertion: Human-collected position-command datasets have jerk spike rate below 2%; scripted/planner-generated datasets regularly exceed this due to sharp trajectory waypoints
claims.conditions: spike defined as per-step jerk norm > 5x median jerk for that episode

evidence.notes: Simulated, 14-DOF bimanual, 50Hz [Corrected 2026-10-19: re-profiled with both grippers excluded (gripper_dims [6, 13]); was 0.0069.]

Scripted ALOHA sim, 14-DOF, 50Hz. Spike rate 24.9% — far above the 2% threshold. Scripted motions have abrupt start/stop profiles not present in human teleop. Does not trigger formal falsification (condition requires hardware dataset) but indicates claim scope should be clarified as 'human-collected' position datasets. [Corrected 2026-10-19: re-profiled with both grippers excluded (gripper_dims [6, 13]); was 0.249.]

Scripted ALOHA sim, 14-DOF, 50Hz. Spike rate 21.9% — consistent with insertion_scripted finding. Confirms that scripted motion planners produce high jerk due to sharp trajectory waypoints. Both scripted datasets disconfirm the claim for scripted (non-human) demonstrations. [Corrected 2026-10-19: re-profiled with both grippers excluded (gripper_dims [6, 13]); was 0.219.]

DROID, 7-DOF position-command, real hardware teleoperation, 15Hz, diverse robots and tasks. Mean spike_rate 4.5% — exceeds the 2% human-teleop threshold and meets the formal falsification condition (rate > 4%). This is the first real-hardware human-teleoperated position-control dataset to challenge JS-001. Likely contributing factors: diverse hardware platforms with varying noise characteristics, 15Hz control loop introducing coarser jerk estimates compared to 50Hz ALOHA, and a wide range of operator skill levels across 100 episodes (episode-level range: 0–13.5%). The claim boundary of 2% appears too tight for diverse real-hardware teleoperation. Evidence now supports revising to ~5% for heterogeneous hardware.

Real hardware mobile ALOHA, 14-DOF, 50Hz, shrimp cooking task, 18 episodes. Spike rate 0.46% — well below 2%. First mobile-ALOHA evidence point; confirms claim holds for mobile-base variants. [Corrected 2026-10-19: re-profiled with both grippers excluded (gripper_dims [6, 13]); was 0.004581.]

Human teleop sim, 14-DOF, 50Hz, cube transfer, 50 episodes. Spike rate 0.94% — below 2%. Consistent with insertion_human (0.69%); confirms claim across ALOHA sim tasks. [Corrected 2026-10-19: re-profiled with both grippers excluded (gripper_dims [6, 13]); was 0.009421.]

Static ALOHA real hardware, 14-DOF, 50Hz, battery task, 49 episodes. Spike rate 0.44% — below 2%. Confirms claim for static-ALOHA real hardware. [Corrected 2026-10-19: re-profiled with both grippers excluded (gripper_dims [6, 13]); was 0.004376.]
Static ALOHA real hardware, 14-DOF, 50Hz, candy task, 50 episodes. Spike rate 0.42% — below 2%. [Corrected 2026-10-19: re-profiled with both grippers excluded (gripper_dims [6, 13]); was 0.004189.]

Static ALOHA real hardware, 14-DOF, 50Hz, coffee task, 50 episodes. Spike rate 0.17% — lowest observed across all human-collected datasets. Coffee prep involves slow, controlled motions. [Corrected 2026-10-19: re-profiled with both grippers excluded (gripper_dims [6, 13]); was 0.001677.]
Static ALOHA real hardware, 14-DOF, 50Hz, cups task, 50 episodes. Spike rate 0.30% — below 2%. [Corrected 2026-10-19: re-profiled with both grippers excluded (gripper_dims [6, 13]); was 0.002972.]

SO-100 low-cost arm, real hardware, position control, pick and place, 50 episodes. Spike rate 1.09% — below 2%, though notably higher than ALOHA. Low-cost arm mechanics (backlash, compliance) contribute to marginally higher spike rate while remaining within the human-teleop threshold.

SO-100 low-cost arm, real hardware, position control, block stacking, 56 episodes. Spike rate 1.02% — below 2%. Consistent with pickplace (1.09%); confirms that low-cost arm hardware stays within the human-teleop threshold.

claims.assertion: Velocity-command datasets have jerk spike rate in the range 2–8% due to frequent direction reversals
claims.conditions: spike defined as per-step jerk norm > 5x median jerk for that episode

evidence.notes: BridgeData V2, 7-DOF real hardware velocity-command, 5Hz, 50415 episodes. Spike rate 0.71% — below the 1% lower falsification threshold. This FORMALLY FALSIFIES JS-002. At 5Hz, the median jerk magnitude within each short episode is elevated, so the 5x-median adaptive threshold is harder to exceed — few individual steps qualify as spikes even when the motion is objectively jerky. This reveals that JS-002's 2–8% range is specific to ~10Hz velocity-command datasets; the spike rate at 5Hz is systematically suppressed by the self-adaptive threshold. The claim must be frequency-qualified. [Corrected 2026-10-20: the reference had computed BridgeData2's smoothness in position mode; in velocity mode on revision b96f7216 the value is 0.81% (was 0.71%). The verdict is unchanged.]

falsification.condition: A second velocity-command dataset with rate < 0.01 or > 0.12
falsification.note: Formally falsified by BridgeData2 (5Hz). JS-002 should be replaced with frequency-qualified successor claims.

claims.assertion: Jerk spike rate is more robust to cross-frequency comparison than LDLJ, because the 5x-median threshold self-adapts to episode scale
claims.conditions: requires same spike_k parameter across datasets being compared

evidence.notes: Same trajectories, only the rate changes (gripper_dims [6, 13]). Spike rate rises 12x from 50 to 10 Hz and crosses the 2% warning level; LDLJ crosses -10 the other way. The 5x-median threshold does not make spike rate frequency-invariant. eval/investigations/ldlj/SUBSAMPLING.md.
Real hardware, gripper_dims [6, 13]. Spike rate 3.4x from 50 to 10 Hz, 7x to 5 Hz; LDLJ moves 4 units. eval/investigations/ldlj/SUBSAMPLING.md.

retracted_evidence.observed: droid_100=4.5% (15Hz, 7D position), aloha=0.35% (50Hz, 12 joint dims, position)
retracted_evidence.notes: First within-control-mode cross-frequency test (position-command, 3.3x frequency ratio). droid_100 (15Hz) spike rate 4.5% vs aloha (50Hz) spike rate 0.69%. Direction matches physical expectation: lower control frequency yields coarser jerk estimates and higher spike rates. The self-adapting 5x-median threshold still captures meaningful per-episode variation at both frequencies, tentatively supporting frequency-robustness. Note: droid_100 hardware noise may also contribute to the higher spike rate, partially confounding the pure frequency effect. [Corrected 2026-10-19: aloha re-profiled with both grippers excluded (gripper_dims [6, 13]); 0.35%, was 0.69%. Direction unchanged.]
retracted_evidence.retraction_reason: Confounded: the datasets differ in sampling rate, action dimensionality and hardware, and the same-trajectory subsampling test shows the difference is explained by sampling rate alone (aloha at 10 Hz reads 4.35%, near pusht's 4.9%; eval/investigations/ldlj/SUBSAMPLING.md). It does not test whether spike rate is more frequency-robust than LDLJ.

retracted_evidence.notes: Within-control-mode (velocity), 2x frequency difference (5Hz vs 10Hz). Spike rates differ 7x (0.71% vs 4.9%), showing the spike rate is highly sensitive to control frequency even within the same class. This CHALLENGES JS-003: the 5x-median adaptive threshold does NOT produce frequency-robust spike rates for velocity-command data across a 2x frequency gap. Frequency must be treated as a confound when comparing spike rates across datasets, even within the same control class.
